Sleep architecture consists of cyclically recurring stages, each characterized by distinct electroencephalographic (EEG) patterns. A typical nocturnal sleep episode comprises 4 to 6 cycles of approximately 90 minutes each. Each cycle progresses through three stages of non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep before entering REM sleep (during which the EEG resembles waking activity, but voluntary skeletal muscles are actively inhibited via glycinergic and GABAergic pathways).

The two-process model of sleep regulation, proposed by Borbely in 1982, posits that sleep propensity is governed by the interaction of a homeostatic process (Process S, which accumulates during waking and dissipates during sleep) and a circadian process (Process C, driven by the suprachiasmatic nucleus). Adenosine, a purine nucleoside that accumulates in the basal forebrain during sustained wakefulness, is the leading candidate for the molecular substrate of Process S. Caffeine exerts its wake-promoting effect precisely by antagonizing adenosine A1 and A2A receptors.

The functional significance of sleep remains incompletely understood, though several hypotheses have empirical support: synaptic homeostasis (the downscaling of potentiated synapses to restore signal-to-noise ratio), metabolic clearance via the glymphatic system (60 percent more active during sleep), and memory consolidation (particularly the transfer of hippocampal traces to neocortical storage during slow-wave sleep).
